definition: The structural core protein of silk; in Bombyx mori it is a complex of heavy and light chains whose glycine- and alanine-rich repeats crystallize into antiparallel beta sheets.
explanation: Each cocoon filament contains two fibroin strands, called brins, cemented together by a coating of sericin. Bombyx mori fibroin combines a very large heavy chain, a much smaller light chain joined to it by a disulfide bond, and a glycoprotein called P25 that associates with the pair without covalent links. The heavy chain is dominated by short repeating motifs of glycine, alanine and serine. As the silkworm spins, these repeats stack into tightly packed beta sheets that form crystalline domains, separated by less regular segments that give the filament some extensibility.
example: A conservator compares a degummed silk thread with a thread of similar diameter under polarized light and sees that the silk glows brightly when rotated at certain angles. The class explains this birefringence as a sign of molecular alignment: beta-sheet crystallites in fibroin lie largely parallel to the filament axis, so light travels differently along the fiber than across it. The same alignment underlies silk's strength along its length.
caution: Fibroin sequences differ between species, so figures for Bombyx mori do not transfer directly to wild silks such as tussah or eri, or to spider silks. Fibroin is also not the whole raw filament: sericin forms a substantial share of cocoon mass until it is removed by degumming. Regenerated fibroin used in biomaterials has been dissolved and reprocessed, so its structure depends on that processing rather than on the silkworm's spinning.
deeper: The Bombyx mori heavy chain has about 5,263 amino acid residues and a mass of roughly 391 kDa, compared with about 26 kDa for the light chain. Its composition is roughly 46% glycine, 30% alanine, 12% serine and 5% tyrosine. The repetitive core consists mainly of the hexapeptides GAGAGS and GAGAGA, with some alanine or serine positions replaced by tyrosine or valine, so the motif can be written broadly as Gly-Ala-Gly-X. Because glycine carries only a hydrogen side chain and alanine a methyl group, adjacent sheets can pack very closely. The stored, unspun form, called silk I, has been assigned a type II beta-turn structure rather than an alpha-helix, while the spun form, silk II, is the antiparallel beta-sheet crystal. Irregular, non-repetitive segments of the heavy chain form the less ordered regions.
origins: The word combines the Latin fibra, fiber, with -in, a common ending for protein names, and it distinguishes the fiber-forming protein from the gummy sericin around it. Silk's diffraction pattern made it a classic example of the extended beta structure first identified in stretched keratin. Detailed sequence knowledge came much later, with the cloning and characterization of the fibroin genes; the structure of the light-chain gene was reported in the early 1990s.

definition: A measure of down's loft: the volume a conditioned sample of down occupies per unit mass under a light standard load, quoted in cubic inches per ounce in US practice.
explanation: Down clusters are plumules in which soft barbs radiate from a small base; their barbules lack the hooklets that zip contour feathers together, so the cluster stays three-dimensional and traps still air. Fill power expresses how much space a given mass of down occupies after it has been conditioned to relax and then compressed gently in a test cylinder under a specified weight. Higher fill power means more volume per unit mass, which usually means more insulation for the weight. Results depend on the method, so values are meaningful only when the test protocol is stated.
example: Two jackets each contain 150 grams of down, one rated 600 fill power and one rated 800 under the same test method. Because 800 divided by 600 is about 1.33, the 800 down occupies about a third more volume and can loft more in the same baffles. A student should still check the down to feather ratio, fill weight and baffle design before assuming the higher-rated jacket is warmer.
caution: Fill power describes loft of the fill, not the warmth of a garment, which also depends on fill weight, construction, shell fabric and fit. Protocols differ in conditioning and apparatus, so results from different methods are not directly interchangeable. Fill power also says nothing about species, feather content, sourcing or animal-welfare practices such as live-plucking.
deeper: In a typical test, a sample of set mass is conditioned so that clusters recover from packing, placed in a transparent cylinder of standard diameter, and loaded with a light piston; after a set time, piston height is read and converted to volume per mass. Loft depends on cluster size and maturity, the proportion of feathers, fibers and broken pieces, residual moisture and oils after washing, and compression history. Wet clusters collapse and lose loft, which is why hydrophobic down treatments exist. Laboratories usually report fill power together with a composition analysis, in which a weighed sample is hand-sorted into down clusters, down fibers, feathers and residue, because a high loft figure means little if the blend is mislabeled.
origins: Fill power arose as bedding and outdoor-equipment makers needed a single number to compare down quality, and the inch-per-ounce unit reflects its adoption in the US market. Composition testing developed alongside it, since loft depends on the share of true down clusters versus feathers and fragments. Industry testing regulations and national standards were written to reduce disagreement between laboratories, but they have not produced one universal protocol.

definition: Fresco is a high-twist, relatively open suiting cloth, usually worsted wool, made for warm-weather wear with a dry, porous hand.
explanation: In mill and tailor language, fresco describes a cloth built from highly twisted worsted yarns set with enough openness that air can move through the fabric. The high twist keeps the yarn springy and helps the cloth resist wrinkling in heat, while the open sett reduces weight and clinging compared with dense tropical plains. Hardy Minnis historically used Fresco as a trademark for such cloths; the same word is now often used generically for similar high-twist tropical suitings from other mills. Treat a hangtag's fresco claim as a construction hint, then confirm fiber, twist character, sett and weight.
example: Hold a fresco-style tropical jacket cloth up to a window beside a dense Super 150s plain weave of similar nominal weight. Light passes more readily through the fresco, and the surface feels drier and more granular because tightly twisted yarns stand slightly apart. On a warm commute the open structure and yarn spring can feel cooler and less creased than a compact, low-twist cloth of the same fiber name.
caution: Fresco is a cloth construction and trade language, not a fiber grade or a Super S number. A fresco label does not prove Australian merino, a particular micron or Hardy Minnis origin. Because Fresco began as a trademark and later entered loose trade use, ask whether the word is a brand name, a mill style name or only a salesperson's shorthand. Open, high-twist cloths can still pill, shine or bag if the finishing and garment design are poor.
deeper: High twist raises the helix angle of fibers in the yarn, increasing yarn compactness and elastic recovery while reducing surface hair, which is why fresco yarns feel dry rather than lofty. An open weave or leno-like openness then lowers cover factor, so thermal and moisture buffering depend on both yarn and sett. The result is often described as tropical suiting: porous enough for warm climates yet formal enough for tailored jackets and trousers. Laboratory comfort claims still need fabric-level air permeability and crease-recovery data; the word fresco alone is not a performance standard. Distinguishing trademark Fresco from generic fresco remains an editorial and commercial question rather than a weave notation in the way 2/2 twill is.
origins: Hardy Minnis of England developed and trademarked Fresco for high-twist tropical wool suitings in the twentieth-century trade, and the cloth became a reference point for warm-weather tailoring. As similar constructions spread among mills, the lower-case word fresco entered buyer vocabulary for open, high-twist worsteds even when the trademark did not apply. Italian and other European tropical lines later offered analogous fabrics under their own style names. The history therefore splits between a protected brand story and a broader construction family that cloth buyers still discuss under the same everyday word.
